a_c.title: THE GREEK LEXICON A–C
a_c.subtitle: Words That Begin Well
a_c.tagline: *Your first vocabulary. Alpha, beta and gamma. The rest will cost you extra.*
a_c.preface_title: A Few Words Before the Words
a_c.preface:
So you've learned the letters. And you've survived the grammar. Frankly, I'm impressed.

Now you'd like to know what the words actually mean. Naturally.

This lexicon covers alpha, beta and gamma. That's three letters out of twenty-four.

I know. But a proper education doesn't come cheap, and I have to split these things up somehow. It keeps the price tolerable. For you. Not for me.

All {n} words in this book appear somewhere in the Gospel of John. I haven't padded it with words you'll never meet. Mostly because then I'd have to look them up.

Each entry gives you the word as a dictionary lists it, its sounds in Latin letters, what kind of word it is, and what it means.

Where a Greek word has several meanings, you get the one that matters most here. The rest you'll have to find out for yourself. Builds character.

You'll notice that many Greek words begin with a tiny mark above the first letter. Those are breathings. They are not contagious.

Right. Off you go.

— John Koine
a_c.outro:
That's alpha, beta and gamma done.

If you're now wondering where the rest of the alphabet went, don't worry. It's in other books. For which you'll need other emeralds.

Further reading, should your purse allow:
a_c.signoff:
**— John Koine**

*P.S. If a word isn't in here, it isn't in John. Or I made a mistake. It's the first one. Probably.*

d_f.title: THE GREEK LEXICON D–F
d_f.subtitle: More Letters, as Promised
d_f.tagline: *Delta, epsilon and zeta. Yes, I did say there would be more letters.*
d_f.preface_title: A Few Words Before the Words
d_f.preface:
You're back. And you brought emeralds. Lovely.

I did mention there would be more letters. Here they are: delta, epsilon and zeta.

Now, the title says D to F. Greek, however, has no letter F. It never did. But "D–F" looked far tidier on the cover, and I decided not to argue with the cover.

Be warned: epsilon is enormous. Well over a hundred words begin with it. I don't know why. Ask the Greeks.

Zeta, on the other hand, has barely eight. The Greeks seem to have run out of enthusiasm somewhere around the sixth letter.

All {n} words here appear in the Gospel of John, and the entries work exactly as in the first book: the word as a dictionary lists it, its sounds in Latin letters, what kind of word it is, and what it means.

If something looks oddly familiar, that's because half your English vocabulary comes from Greek. You're welcome.

Carry on.

— John Koine
d_f.outro:
That's delta, epsilon and zeta.

Eighteen letters are still waiting. I'm not saying you need them. I'm just saying they exist.

Where to find them:
d_f.signoff:
**— John Koine**

*P.S. Yes, epsilon really is that long. No, I did not count them twice.*

thematic.title: THE THEMATIC GREEK LEXICON
thematic.subtitle: Words Sorted by What They're About
thematic.tagline: *For people who know what they want to say but not how to say it. Or who are simply tired of the alphabet.*
thematic.preface_title: A Few Words Before the Words
thematic.preface:
An alphabetical lexicon is wonderful if you already know the word. But if you already know the word, you don't need a lexicon.

That's the problem.

This book solves it. Instead of the alphabet, the words are sorted by what they're about. Light and darkness. Food. Family. Walking about. You know, the usual.

Every one of the {n} words from the Gospel of John appears here exactly once. Not twice. I'm not made of ink.

If you can't find a word in the theme where you expect it, try another. Greek words have a habit of wandering.

And if you still can't find it, check the Little Words. Everything small ends up there.

Each entry works as in the other lexica: the word, its sounds in Latin letters, what kind of word it is, and what it means.

Within a theme, the words are sorted by their Latin spelling, so you needn't know the Greek alphabet to find anything. Although it helps. It always helps.

Happy browsing.

— John Koine
thematic.outro:
That's the Gospel of John in twenty-one piles.

If you'd rather have your words in alphabetical order, there are the lexica A–C and D–F.

And if you'd like both orders in one book, the Complete Greek Lexicon contains this one. And all the others.

I'd call it a bargain. Others might call it a lot of emeralds. Both are true.

See for yourself:
thematic.signoff:
**— John Koine**

*P.S. Yes, "Everyday Actions" is a bit of a dumping ground. Life is like that.*

complete.title: THE COMPLETE GREEK LEXICON
complete.subtitle: Every Word of the Gospel of John, Twice
complete.tagline: *In order of the alphabet and in order of subject. Because you finally have the emeralds.*
complete.preface:
Well, well. Look who finally has some emeralds.

I remember you. You were the one with the Alphabet Primer who couldn't quite afford the rest. I told you that a proper education doesn't come cheap.

You didn't believe me.

And now here you are, holding the Complete Greek Lexicon.

Every word of the Gospel of John, from alpha to omega. All {n} of them. Twice, actually: once in the order of the alphabet and once sorted by subject.

That's the Greek Lexicon A–C, the Greek Lexicon D–F and the Thematic Greek Lexicon in one handsome volume.

Between you and me, those who bought the little ones separately will feel slightly foolish about it. I'd have mentioned it sooner. But then I'd have had to give up the emeralds.

Take your time with it. It's heavy, for a book. Possibly because it's made entirely of value for money.

Now, if you'll excuse me, I have some emeralds to count.

— John Koine
complete.key_intro:
{n} words. Each entry gives the word as a dictionary lists it, its sounds in Latin letters, what kind of word it is and what it means.

Where a word has several senses, you get the one that matters most in John. For the others, you'll need a proper scholar.

The little marks:
complete.part_one:
Part One lists every word in the order of the Greek alphabet. Each letter begins on a new page.

Alpha is huge. Omega is tiny. Life isn't fair, and neither is the Greek alphabet.
complete.part_two:
Part Two lists the very same words again, sorted by what they're about. Light, food, family, walking around.

Twenty-one little chapters. Useful when you know what you want to say but not what it's called.

Within a chapter, the words are sorted by their Latin spelling.
complete.outro:
That's everything.

Every word in the Gospel of John, twice, with a preface and an unreasonable number of emeralds behind it.

If you've read this from alpha to omega, you're either a scholar or in need of fresh air. Possibly both.

Either way, you can now open the Gospel and know what the words mean. Whether you know what they're doing there is a question for the Grammar Book.

I did tell you to read it.
complete.signoff:
**— John Koine**

*P.S. No refunds. The Scribe was most insistent.*
